new_statements.quote: 1.2 Stress. The main lexical HSF stress is regular, and commonly falls on the (first) long vowel (HSF stress seems to be attracted by a heavy syllable). If there is no long vowel in a word, then the accent is on the first short vowel. This rule has already been proposed by Larsen and Pike (1949) for San Luis Potosí Huastec. ['ʔuxum] uxum woman; [manu'nu:l] manunuul yellow; [ta'ta:ʔ] tataa' you, 2sg; ['tamup] tamup year; [ɓaθi'θi:l] bathithiil straight; ['kamap] kamap tooth. In South Eastern Huastec two long vowels normally do not occur in one word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive: primary word stress falls on the syllable with a long vowel (normally the only one in the word; Kondic says 'the (first) long vowel'). If the word has no long vowel, stress falls on the first (leftmost) short vowel, i.e. the initial syllable. Coda consonants do not count as weight. Stressed vowels of Spanish loans are lengthened, so loans conform to the rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Kondic notes two long vowels normally do not co-occur in a word except when the reciprocal -VVx or stative participle -VVm lengthens the root vowel (sec. 1.6); she does not say which long vowel is stressed in that case beyond '(first) long vowel'.
new_statements.exceptions: Preposed person-marking clitics (absolutive/ergative/inverse) are never stressed and are written separately so they do not interfere with the rule (p. 49: k-u tuj-uw ['tujuw] 'that I start it'). Intonational/focus stress can fall on a clause-final focused word (pp. on information structure). Loans: stressed vowel lengthened.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress ('main lexical HSF stress'); domain is the phonological word excluding the preposed person clitics. Comparative restatement p. 398: 'the stress in these languages falls on the first long vowel; if there are no long vowels in a word, the stress falls on the first short vowel', said to hold for all three Huastec varieties (Larsen & Pike 1949 for SLP, Constable 1989 for Veracruz).
new_statements.identity_note: huas1256 is a Glottolog bookkeeping code for ISO [hsf] "Southeastern Huastec", retired by ISO CR 2008-051 (2009-01-16) into [hus] Huastec (huas1242). The statement quoted is first-hand for exactly this variety: Kondic 2012 calls it "South Eastern Huastec (HSF)", spoken in the Sierra de Otontepec, northern Veracruz (Chontla, Tantima, Tancoco, Chinampa, Naranjos, Amatlan, Tamiahua per Kaufman 1985 as cited on pp. 22-23; fieldwork base San Francisco Chontla), and distinguishes it from Veracruz/Tantoyuca Huastec (old HUS) and San Luis Potosí Huastec (old HVA). The earlier scan's es.wikipedia quote and the Meléndez 2017 / Herrera Zendejas 2014 / Larsen & Pike 1949 statements are about the other two dialects (Tantoyuca and SLP), not this one. Kondic 2012 p. 398 states the rule is the same across all three varieties.

readall_conflicts: No catalog record exists for huas1256. The one work of this item, Larsen & Pike 1949, is open held by the project (archive.org scanned of Language vol. 25) and was read in full: it treats San Luis Potosí Huastec (Otoñiel Oyarvide near Tamazunchale), not Southeastern Huastec, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the statement held by the project for this key directly. It does expose a discrepancy in the literature chain: Larsen & Pike place stress on the LAST long vowel of the word (else the first vowel), while Kondic 2012 (pp. 48, 398), the source of the statement held by the project, gives the SE Huastec rule as the '(first) long vowel', else the first short vowel, and says this is the rule Larsen & Pike proposed; Meléndez Guadarrama 2017 restates it the same way, whereas Hagberg (via Hayes 1981) and Bennett 2016 report Larsen & Pike's 'rightmost long vowel' correctly. Both versions are weight-sensitive unbounded systems with initial default; they differ only for words containing two or more long vowels, and the examples carried in the statement held by the project (uxum, manunuul, tataa', tamup, bathithiil) each contain at most one long vowel, so as quoted they do not decide between first and last.

sources.citation: Meléndez Guadarrama, Lucero. 2017. Huasteco de El Mamey, Tantoyuca, Veracruz (Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México). México: El Colegio de México. 'Acento' pp. 36-37.
sources.note: pp. 36-37: 'el acento en huasteco de El Mamey, Tantoyuca, no es fonológico.. en palabras de dos o más sílabas, el acento recae en la sílaba que tiene un núcleo vocálico complejo. Cuando no hay longitud, el acento tiende a recaer en la primera sílaba a la izquierda de la palabra', crediting Larsen & Pike 1949. Veracruz/Tantoyuca dialect (old HUS), not the Southeastern variety.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514. doi 10.1111/lnc3.12148.
sources.note: p. 496: 'In Huastec, stress falls on the rightmost long vowel, otherwise on the initial syllable (Larsen & Pike 1949, Edmonson 1988, Herrera Zendejas 2011; cf. Herrera Zendejas 2014:Ch.7 for apparent counter-examples)'. Second-hand survey, generic Huastec.

sources.citation: Herrera Zendejas, Esther. 2014. Mapa fónico de las lenguas mexicanas: formas sonoras 1 y 2. México: El Colegio de México. Cap. 7 'Patrones fónicos del huasteco', 'Patrón acentual' pp. 272-281.
sources.note: p. 275: CV and CVC count the same (codas weightless), pattern is trochaic strong-weak, and 'la lengua es sensible a la cantidad, ya que si hay una sílaba con vocal larga, ésta atrae el acento'; data from Tancanhuitz, San Luis Potosí (Potosino dialect), not the Southeastern variety.
